lessons.title: Overview of Cassava Processing Steps
lessons.body:
Cassava roots start spoiling within 24 to 48 hours after harvest. To turn them into safe, storable food, you must process them quickly. The main steps are: peeling, washing, chipping or grating, dewatering, sieving, drying, and sometimes milling or frying. Each step removes water or toxins and changes the texture for the next stage. For example, fresh roots contain about 60-70% water. After processing into gari or flour, moisture drops to 10-12%. That is why drying is critical.

In Africa, most processing is done by hand or with small machines. A typical day for a family might start with harvesting 200 kg of roots. They peel by hand with knives, wash in basins or drums, then grate using a motorized grater (often 5-10 HP). The grated pulp is pressed in a hydraulic jack or screw press to remove excess water. Then it is sieved to break lumps and finally dried on a concrete floor, solar dryer, or mechanical dryer. The whole process can take 1-3 days depending on weather and equipment.

Different end products need different steps. For gari, after pressing you ferment for 1-3 days, then sieve, fry in a hot pan with palm oil, and sieve again. For cassava flour, you skip fermentation, press, dry, and mill. For chips, you slice roots into pieces and dry them directly. Always use fresh roots; discard any that are soft, moldy, or smell bad. Also, never eat raw cassavaâit contains cyanide that must be removed by soaking, fermenting, or drying. Proper processing makes cassava safe and profitable. Start with small batches to learn the timing, then scale up as you master each step.

lessons.title: Peeling, Washing, and Chipping
lessons.body:
Peeling is the first hands-on step. Use a sharp knife with a short blade, like a kitchen knife or machete. Hold the root firmly and cut off both ends, then slit the skin lengthwise and peel it away. The outer brown skin and the inner pinkish layer must be removed because they contain most of the cyanide. A skilled person can peel 50-80 kg per hour. For large-scale, you can buy a motorized peeler (cost: $500-$2000) that rubs roots against rough surfaces, but hand peeling is still common in Africa.

After peeling, wash the roots in clean water. Use a large basin, drum, or concrete tank. Change the water oftenâdirty water spreads bacteria. For 100 kg of roots, use about 200 liters of water. Scrub with your hands or a soft brush to remove dirt and remaining skin. If you plan to make chips, you can skip washing and just peel, but washing improves quality.

Chipping means cutting roots into small pieces, usually 2-5 cm thick. Use a sharp knife or a mechanical chipper. Chips dry faster than whole roots. Spread chips in a thin layer (5-10 cm deep) on a drying rack or clean concrete. In sunny weather, 100 kg of fresh chips will dry to about 30-35 kg in 2-3 days. Turn them twice a day. If it rains, cover them or move them under a shelter. Chips are ready when they snap easily and are brittle. Store dried chips in jute bags in a dry room. They can be milled into flour or sold to processors. Always wear gloves when peeling to avoid skin irritation from cassava juice.

lessons.title: Grating and Pulping Techniques
lessons.body:
Grating turns peeled roots into a fine pulp. This breaks cell walls and releases enzymes that help remove cyanide during fermentation. The traditional method uses a hand grater (a piece of tin with punched holes nailed to a board). It is slowâonly 10-15 kg per hourâand hard on the hands. Better is a motorized grater. In many African markets, you can buy a locally made grater for $300-$800. It has a rotating drum with sharp teeth, powered by a 5-10 HP diesel or electric motor. It can grate 500-1000 kg per hour.

To grate, feed roots into the hopper while the machine runs. Mix in a little water to prevent clogging. The pulp comes out as a wet mash. For gari, you want a fine, uniform pulp. For other products like fufu, a coarser grate is okay. After grating, you can add a starter culture (like a spoonful of old fermented pulp) to speed up fermentation and improve flavor. Let the pulp sit in a clean container for 1-3 days. It will ferment, sour, and release water. This fermentation reduces cyanide by 80-95%.

If you don't have a machine, you can use a pulping method: soak peeled roots in water for 3-4 days until soft, then mash them with a pestle and mortar or squeeze them by hand. This is labor-intensive but works for small quantities. Always keep the grating area clean. Wash the machine after each use to prevent mold and bacteria. Wear a nose mask if the pulp smells strong. After grating, move quickly to pressingâdon't let the pulp sit too long before pressing, or it may spoil.

lessons.title: Dewatering and Pressing Methods
lessons.body:
After grating or fermenting, the pulp contains 60-70% water. You must remove most of it to get a dry, stable product. Pressing does two things: it squeezes out water and helps compact the pulp into a cake. The traditional method is to put the pulp in a woven bag (like a polypropylene sack) and place heavy stones on top. This works but is slowâit can take 12-24 hours to press 50 kg. A better method is a screw press or hydraulic jack press. A simple screw press costs $200-$500 and can press 100 kg in 30-60 minutes. A hydraulic jack press (using a 10-20 ton jack) costs $500-$1500 and is faster.

To press, fill a clean sack with fermented pulp, tie it tightly, and place it in the press. Apply pressure gradually. Water will run out. Collect the waterâit can be used for animal feed or fertilizer after treatment. Press until the cake is firm and no more water drips. For gari, you want the cake to be about 40-50% moisture. For flour, press harder to get 30-40% moisture. If you press too hard, you may lose starch in the water, so don't overdo it.

After pressing, the cake is ready for sieving or drying. If you don't have a press, you can use a dewatering machine (also called a presser) that combines grinding and pressing. In some areas, you can rent a press from a local cooperative for $5-$10 per batch. Always press on a clean surface, like a concrete floor or a plastic sheet, to avoid contamination. Wear gloves and wash hands after handling the wet cake. Proper pressing saves drying time and fuel.

lessons.title: Sieving and Particle Size Reduction
lessons.body:
Sieving breaks up the pressed cake into small, uniform particles. This is important for even drying and for the final texture of your product. For gari, you sieve after pressing and before frying. For flour, you sieve after drying and before milling. The traditional sieve is a woven basket or a mesh screen (like a mosquito net) stretched over a wooden frame. A standard sieve has holes of 2-5 mm. You can buy a set of sieves for $20-$50.

To sieve, rub the pressed cake through the sieve with your hands or a wooden paddle. The fine particles fall through; the lumps stay on top and are rubbed again. For 100 kg of wet cake, sieving takes 1-2 hours by hand. A motorized sieve (vibrating screen) costs $500-$1500 and can sieve 500 kg per hour. It is worth it if you process more than 500 kg per day. After sieving, you get a fluffy, uniform mash. For gari, you then fry this mash in a hot pan with a little palm oil. For flour, you spread the sieved mash on a drying tray.

Particle size matters. For gari, you want a medium-coarse grain (like semolina). For fufu flour, you want a fine powder (like wheat flour). You can adjust by using different sieve sizes. Always sieve in a clean, dust-free area. Cover the sieved product with a clean cloth to keep off flies and dust. If you are making chips, you skip sievingâchips are already in pieces. After sieving, move quickly to drying or frying to prevent spoilage. Clean your sieves after each use with water and a brush, then dry them in the sun.

lessons.title: Drying Methods: Sun, Solar, and Mechanical
lessons.body:
Drying is the most critical step to preserve cassava products. Fresh processed cassava has 40-60% moisture. You must bring it down to 10-12% for safe storage. There are three main methods: sun drying, solar drying, and mechanical drying. Each has pros and cons.

Sun drying is the cheapest. Spread the product (chips, sieved mash, or grated pulp) on a clean concrete floor, black plastic sheet, or woven mat. Use a thin layer (2-5 cm). In full sun (30-35Â°C), it takes 2-3 days for chips, 1-2 days for gari mash. Turn the product every 2-3 hours with a rake or wooden paddle. Protect from rain and animals. Sun drying is free but slow and risky in rainy season. It also exposes food to dust and insects.

Solar drying uses a solar dryerâa box with a glass or plastic top and ventilation holes. The temperature inside can reach 50-70Â°C, so drying is 2-3 times faster than sun. A small solar dryer (1-2 mÂ²) costs $100-$300 and can dry 20-50 kg per batch. It protects from rain, dust, and animals. You can build one with local materials: wooden frame, clear polythene sheet, and black painted interior. Mechanical drying uses a fuel or electric dryer. A small mechanical dryer costs $500-$2000 and can dry 100-500 kg per batch in 4-8 hours. It is best for large-scale or rainy season. But it needs fuel (diesel, gas, or electricity), which adds cost.

Whichever method, test for dryness: a dried chip should snap, not bend. Dried gari should be crispy. Store dried products in airtight containers or jute bags in a dry, cool room. Never store while still warmâlet it cool first. Proper drying stops mold and keeps your cassava safe for months.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cassava Processing â Primary Operations

For African cassava processors â from village-level garri and fufu makers to emerging commercial starch and flour enterprises â the primary processing steps (peeling through drying) determine product quality, shelf life, and ultimately price. This practical reference consolidates the operational parameters, equipment choices, and quality checkpoints you need to run a profitable cassava processing line. Every kilogram of fresh roots contains 60â70% moisture and must be transformed within 24â48 hours of harvest to avoid spoilage and cyanogenic glycoside accumulation. The decisions you make at each step â from peeling method to drying technology â directly affect your yield, your costs, and your market access.

Step-by-Step Operational Parameters

Cassava processing follows two main routes: the dry route (peeling â washing â chipping â drying â milling) for chips and flour, and the wet route (peeling â washing â grating â dewatering â sieving/pulping â drying/frying) for garri, fufu, and starch. Your choice depends on your target market and capital. The dry route requires less water and simpler equipment; the wet route commands higher prices for fermented products like garri but demands more labour and processing infrastructure.

At every stage, time and hygiene are your most valuable assets. Fresh roots begin deteriorating within 24 hours of harvest. Cyanogenic glycosides â naturally present in cassava â are reduced through peeling, soaking, fermentation, and drying. Inadequate processing leaves residual cyanide, which is both a health hazard and a market barrier. The tables below give you the concrete numbers to plan your operations and train your staff.

Table 1: Primary Processing Operations â Key Parameters and Equipment
Operation Key Parameter Typical Equipment Throughput (small-scale) Critical Quality Check
Peeling Remove 1â2 mm outer skin + 2â3 mm cortex; 85â90% peel removal efficiency Manual knives; mechanical peelers (abrasive or knife type) 50â80 kg/hr (manual); 500â1,000 kg/hr (mechanical) No visible brown/black specks; minimal flesh loss
Washing Water-to-root ratio 3:1; 2â3 rinse cycles; final rinse water clear Immersion tanks; rotary washer; spray washer 200â500 kg/hr No sand/grit; no residual soil odour
Chipping Chip thickness 2â5 cm; uniform size for even drying Manual chipping knives; motorised chipper 100â300 kg/hr Uniform thickness; no mashed or crushed chips
Grating Particle size 0.5â2 mm; rasp or hammer mill at 1,500â3,000 rpm Motorised grater; hammer mill 300â800 kg/hr Smooth paste; no large uncooked chunks
Dewatering Moisture reduction from ~65% to 45â50%; pressure 5â10 tonnes Manual screw press; hydraulic press; centrifuge 100â400 kg/hr Firm cake; no free water; consistent moisture
Sieving Mesh size 0.5â2 mm; reject rate <5% Vibrating sieve; rotary sifter; manual screen 200â600 kg/hr Uniform granule size; no fibre clumps
Drying (sun) 2â4 days; 8â10 hrs/day; turning every 2 hrs; final moisture <12% Concrete drying floor; raised racks 50â100 kg/batch Brittle chips; no mould; uniform colour
Drying (solar) 1â2 days; cabinet temperature 40â60Â°C; final moisture <12% Solar cabinet dryer; greenhouse dryer 100â500 kg/batch No condensation; even drying; no case-hardening
Drying (mechanical) 6â12 hrs; inlet air 60â80Â°C; final moisture <12% Rotary dryer; tray dryer; flash dryer 500â2,000 kg/batch Consistent moisture; no scorching; low energy cost/kg

Sources: FAO (2001), Cassava Processing, Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 148; NSPRI (2020), Cassava Value Addition Technologies; IITA (2019), Cassava Processing Equipment Catalogue.

Table 2: Cost and Revenue Comparison â Small-Scale vs. Medium-Scale Processing (per tonne fresh roots)
Cost/Revenue Item Small-Scale (Manual) Medium-Scale (Semi-Mechanised) Notes
Fresh roots purchase USD 80â120 USD 80â120 Farm-gate price varies by country/season
Labour (processing) USD 40â60 USD 15â25 Mechanisation reduces labour by 50â60%
Energy/Fuel USD 5â10 USD 30â50 Mechanical drying adds fuel cost but speeds cycle
Water USD 5â8 USD 10â15 Wet route uses 3â5Ã more water
Equipment depreciation USD 5â10 USD 20â35 Based on 3â5 year lifespan
Packaging USD 10â15 USD 15â25 Food-grade bags/containers
Total Cost USD 145â223 USD 170â270 Per tonne fresh roots processed
Dried chips yield 250â280 kg 280â300 kg Mechanisation improves yield by 5â10%
Market price (chips) USD 0.80â1.20/kg USD 0.80â1.20/kg Regional variation; quality premium possible
Gross Revenue (chips) USD 200â336 USD 224â360 Based on yield Ã price range
Gross Margin (chips) USD 55â113 USD 54â90 Small-scale can be competitive on margin
Garri revenue (wet route) USD 300â450 USD 350â500 Higher value but more processing steps
Garri gross margin USD 100â200 USD 120â230 Fermentation and frying add value

Sources: Compiled from IITA (2019) Cassava Processing Equipment Catalogue; FAO (2001) Cassava Processing; and West Africa cassava market surveys (2022â2023). Prices are indicative and vary by country, season, and exchange rate. Processors should recalculate with local figures.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â CYANIDE AND MECHANICAL HAZARDS

Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin and lotaustralin). Improper processing â especially insufficient soaking, fermentation, or drying â can leave dangerous residual cyanide. Never consume or sell cassava products that have not been adequately processed. Symptoms of cyanide poisoning include headache, dizziness, nausea, and in severe cases, respiratory failure. Additionally, mechanical graters, presses, and chippers cause severe injuries if operated without guards. Always use push-sticks, never hands, to feed machines. Ensure adequate ventilation when drying mechanically â cyanide gas can accumulate in enclosed drying rooms. Train all staff on emergency shutdown procedures and keep a first-aid kit on site.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Root freshness: Process within 24â48 hours of harvest; reject roots with soft spots, mould, or offensive odour.
  • Peeling quality: Remove all outer skin and cortex; aim for 85â90% peel removal with minimal flesh loss.
  • Washing efficiency: Use at least 3:1 water-to-root ratio; final rinse water must be clear; remove all sand and grit.
  • Chip uniformity: Cut chips 2â5 cm thick for even drying; avoid mashed or crushed pieces that invite mould.
  • Grating consistency: Achieve 0.5â2 mm particle size; check for uncooked chunks that reduce product quality.
  • Dewatering target: Reduce moisture to 45â50%; cake should be firm with no free water when squeezed.
  • Drying endpoint: Dry to <12% moisture; chips should snap cleanly, not bend; test with moisture meter if available.
  • Hygiene and safety: Wash equipment between batches; use machine guards; never touch moving parts; store dried product in airtight, food-grade containers.

Further Reading â Free Official Resources

  1. FAO â Cassava Processing (Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 148) â Comprehensive guide covering all primary and secondary processing steps, equipment, and quality standards. Free full text online.
  2. IITA â Cassava Research and Processing Resources â Technical bulletins, equipment catalogues, and best-practice guides for African cassava value chains. Free downloads.
  3. Nigerian Stored Products Research Institute (NSPRI) â Post-harvest and processing technologies for cassava, including dryer designs and storage guidelines. Free technical publications.
  4. CGIAR â Cassava Processing and Value Addition â Research papers and practical guides on cassava processing in sub-Saharan Africa. Open access.
  5. African Cassava Initiative â Technical Resources â Training materials, business models, and market information for cassava processors across Africa. Free registration for full access.

Business bottom line: Primary processing is where you either capture value or lose it. A well-run peeling and drying operation can turn USD 100 of fresh roots into USD 250â350 of dried chips or flour. The key is consistency â uniform chips, proper moisture control, and hygienic handling. Invest in a moisture meter (USD 30â80) and a simple screw press (USD 200â500) before you scale up. These two tools alone can improve your yield by 10â15% and your product price by 20% through better quality. Start small, measure everything, and reinvest your margins into the next processing step.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time you should wait after harvesting cassava roots before processing?
quiz.explanation: Cassava roots start spoiling within 24-48 hours, so processing must begin quickly.

quiz.q: Which part of the cassava root contains most of the cyanide?
options: B) The outer brown skin and inner pinkish layer
quiz.explanation: The skin and the layer just beneath it contain the highest concentration of cyanide.

quiz.q: What is the typical moisture content of fresh cassava roots?
quiz.explanation: Fresh cassava roots contain about 60-70% water, which must be removed during processing.

quiz.q: Which tool is traditionally used for grating cassava?
options: B) A hand grater made from punched tin
quiz.explanation: A hand grater made from a piece of tin with punched holes is a common traditional tool.

quiz.q: How long should you ferment grated cassava pulp for gari to reduce cyanide?
quiz.explanation: Fermentation for 1-3 days reduces cyanide by 80-95% and improves flavor.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of pressing the grated cassava pulp?
quiz.explanation: Pressing squeezes out water, making the pulp easier to dry and process further.

quiz.q: Which of these is a traditional method for dewatering cassava pulp?
options: B) Placing heavy stones on a sack of pulp
quiz.explanation: Placing heavy stones on a sack of pulp is a simple traditional pressing method.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for dried cassava chips for safe storage?
quiz.explanation: Drying to 10-12% moisture prevents mold and spoilage during storage.

quiz.q: Which sieving method is best for large-scale processing (over 500 kg per day)?
options: A) Hand sieving with a basket
quiz.explanation: A motorized vibrating screen can sieve 500 kg per hour, much faster than hand sieving.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of solar drying over sun drying?
options: B) It is faster and protects from rain and dust
quiz.explanation: Solar dryers reach higher temperatures and protect the product from weather and contaminants.

quiz.q: How can you test if cassava chips are fully dried?
options: B) They snap easily and are brittle
quiz.explanation: Fully dried chips are brittle and snap, indicating low moisture.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after grating cassava roots?
options: A) Let it sit for a day
B) Press it to remove water
C) Dry it in the sun
quiz.explanation: After grating, pressing should follow soon to prevent spoilage and remove excess water.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a step in cassava processing for gari?
quiz.explanation: Gari production does not involve boiling whole roots; it uses grated and fermented pulp.

quiz.q: What is the typical capacity of a motorized cassava grater?
quiz.explanation: A motorized grater with a 5-10 HP motor can grate 500-1000 kg per hour.

quiz.q: Why is it important to wash peeled cassava roots before processing?
options: B) To remove dirt and bacteria
quiz.explanation: Washing removes dirt, bacteria, and remaining skin, improving product quality.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for cassava chips for drying?
quiz.explanation: Chips of 2-5 cm thickness dry efficiently without taking too long.

quiz.q: Which pressing method is fastest for 100 kg of pulp?
quiz.explanation: A hydraulic jack press can press 100 kg in 30-60 minutes, faster than other methods.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of sieving after pressing?
options: B) To break lumps and make uniform particles
quiz.explanation: Sieving breaks up the pressed cake into small, uniform particles for even drying and texture.

quiz.q: Which drying method is most suitable for rainy season?
quiz.explanation: Mechanical drying works regardless of weather, making it reliable in rainy season.

quiz.q: How often should you turn cassava chips during sun drying?
quiz.explanation: Turning every 2-3 hours ensures even drying and prevents mold.

quiz.q: What is a sign that fermented cassava pulp is ready for pressing?
options: B) It has a sour smell and released water
quiz.explanation: Fermentation produces a sour smell and releases water, indicating readiness.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety precaution when peeling cassava?
quiz.explanation: Gloves protect hands from skin irritation caused by cassava juice.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a small solar dryer?
quiz.explanation: A small solar dryer (1-2 mÂ²) costs between $100 and $300.

quiz.q: What should you do with the water squeezed out during pressing?
options: B) Use it for animal feed or fertilizer
D) Add it back to the pulp
quiz.explanation: The pressed water contains nutrients and can be used for animal feed or fertilizer after treatment.

quiz.q: Which cassava product requires fermentation before drying?
quiz.explanation: Gari production includes a fermentation step after grating and before pressing.

quiz.q: What is the main disadvantage of sun drying?
options: C) It is slow and risky in rainy season
quiz.explanation: Sun drying depends on weather and can take several days, with risk of rain spoilage.

quiz.q: How can you build a simple solar dryer with local materials?
options: A) Use a wooden frame, clear polythene sheet, and black painted interior
B) Use a metal box with glass
quiz.explanation: A wooden frame covered with clear polythene and painted black inside absorbs heat for drying.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sieve hole size for gari?
quiz.explanation: A sieve with 2-5 mm holes produces the desired medium-coarse gari grain.

quiz.q: Why should you not store dried cassava products while still warm?
quiz.explanation: Warm products create condensation, leading to mold growth during storage.

quiz.q: Which step comes immediately after peeling and washing in cassava processing?
quiz.explanation: After peeling and washing, roots are either grated or chipped, depending on the end product.
